abstract: Cosolvent effects on protein fold stability are widely studied, whereas their role in regulating protein assembly remains less characterized. Here, we explore the additive transfer formalism to quantify the free energy of disassembly of crystal protein self-assemblies in response to cosolvents and compare it with protein denaturation. Using crystal structures of hundreds of assemblies from the Protein Data Bank, we obtain m-values for disassembly and denaturation in urea, betaine, proline, sorbitol, sucrose, sarcosine, and TMAO. Disassembly m-values are about 1 order of magnitude smaller than denaturation m-values, consistently with the smaller surface area exposed during this process. The magnitude of the disassembly m-values increases with the number of exposed residues, but at comparable contact numbers they are not uniquely determined by exposed surface area, indicating regulation by the physicochemical composition of protein-protein contacts. In contrast, denaturation shows a greater correlation with raw residue exposure upon unfolding. Thus, compared to denaturation, disassembly is more strongly regulated by the residue composition of protein-protein contacts than by the raw exposed area. Correlations between disassembly m-values and residue type are opposite for urea relative to the other cosolvents. Betaine and proline tend to promote crystal disassembly, but in a highly composition-dependent manner. The classification of the cosolvents according to their thermodynamic effects in disassembly and denaturation provides a basis for identifying conditions that stabilize assemblies while preserving native monomer structures. This is essential for regulating the biological function of assemblies and dense protein aggregates. The methods to compute solvent accessible surface area and m-values, supporting periodic boundary conditions, are available in the free, open-source, PDBTools.jl package, and can be used to understand cosolvent effects on general protein structural transformations.
